data.title: Crude Futures Post Back-to-Back Weekly Losses — 2nd Update
data.description:
By Farhan Rafid and Anthony Harrup

Oil futures fell for a second consecutive week, while traders assessed the International Energy Agency's outlook for a global supply surplus, continued disruptions to Middle Eastern oil shipments, and cooling expectations for a negotiated settlement between the U.S. and Iran.

Front-month Brent crude for January delivery settled at $95.84 a barrel on Friday, up two cents on the day and down 2.5% from a week ago. West Texas Intermediate for December delivery slipped 0.2% to $88.56 a barrel for a 2.5% weekly loss.

The International Energy Agency said Friday that the global oil market is expected to return to a surplus in the fourth quarter for the first time since the Iran war began, as a recovery in Middle Eastern exports outpaces demand.

Global oil supply rose by 2.3 million barrels a day to 105.4 million barrels a day in October, prompting the Paris-based agency to raise its fourth-quarter supply estimate by 3.3 million barrels a day. Gulf oil exports excluding Oman reached 18.4 million barrels a day, about 26% below prewar levels.

The agency also reported the first monthly increase in observed global oil inventories since June, with stocks rising by 52 million barrels in October. However, inventories remained 462 million barrels below their levels at the start of the war.

Oil futures rebounded Thursday after President Trump said Washington no longer needed an agreement with Iran, raising questions about the prospects for negotiations. Trump also said in a Truth Social post that the U.S. had secured control of the Strait of Hormuz.

"Oil prices have come off really quite significantly, even with the uptick of the last couple of days," said Ellen Fraser, a partner and energy analyst at consulting firm Baringa. But the decline has been sentiment-driven, which "in itself is a bit of a warning."

The northern hemisphere is heading for a tight winter with prices still well above pre-war levels, Fraser added. "There's still a lot of tension and stress in the market."

ING analysts said recovering Middle Eastern production had eased immediate supply concerns, although reliance on alternative export routes continued to leave shipments vulnerable to disruption. The pace at which traffic through the Strait of Hormuz returns to normal remains a key factor for oil prices, they said.

Oil markets may be pricing in the prospect of diplomatic progress before additional supplies become available, according to Terri-Leigh Bennett, chief operating officer at CMS Prime. Negotiations wouldn't immediately restore damaged infrastructure, normalize shipping routes or guarantee uninterrupted production, she said.

Security risks persisted across the region. The Bahrain-based Joint Maritime Information Center, a multinational maritime security monitoring body, said in an advisory distributed Thursday by U.K. Maritime Trade Operations that it had recorded 181 maritime security incidents since March 1, including four since its previous report published Sunday.

Oil shipments through the Strait of Hormuz also remained sharply below prewar levels, with confirmed transits averaging 4.06 million barrels a day in the latest weekly data available Wednesday, compared with 17.1 million barrels a day before the conflict, according to preliminary Kpler data.

The IEA expects global oil demand to fall by 2.7 million barrels a day this year before rebounding by 2 million barrels a day in 2027. It warned that further attacks on shipping could undermine the recovery in oil flows.

Write to Farhan Rafid at farhan.rafid@wsj.com and Anthony Harrup at anthony.harrup@wsj.com

data.title: Soybean futures set two-week high, wheat rises from June low
data.description:
By Tom Polansek

Chicago Board of Trade soybean futures set a two-week high on Friday and corn futures also advanced as traders refocused on tightened US supply forecasts.

US export demand helped support prices, traders said.

The US Department of Agriculture lowered its projection for 2026/27 soybean ending stocks in a monthly report on Tuesday, when analysts were expecting an increase, and raised its outlook for US exports. It also pegged US corn stocks below analysts' expectations.

"We're still digesting the report from earlier in the week," said Matt Wiegand, commodity broker for FuturesOne. "We got friendlier carryout numbers on corn and beans."

The USDA on Friday reported that exporters sold US soybeans to China, Vietnam and unknown destinations and US corn to Mexico. The agency separately said 2026/27 US corn export sales were 2.9 million metric tons for the week that ended on November 5, toward the high end of analysts' expectations.

CBOT January soybeans finished 12-1/2 cents higher at $12.31-1/2 per bushel and reached the highest level since October 30. December corn futures ended 3 cents higher at $4.45-1/2 per bushel.

Wheat also advanced, with December futures closing up 9 cents at $5.93-1/4 per bushel on the CBOT.

Technical buying helped lift wheat prices after the most-active contract touched its lowest level since June 30, traders said. Some traders said losses on Thursday had been overdone.

"Grains are bouncing strongly after yesterday's sharp selloff," said Andrey Sizov, head of consultancy Sovecon.

Traders monitored continued disruptions to Black Sea grain exports, despite diplomatic efforts to end Russia's war with Ukraine.

With no sign of progress in Russia-Ukraine talks toward a ceasefire in the Black Sea, limited shipments should support wheat prices, Sizov said. He added that competitively priced new-crop Argentine wheat could remain a cap on prices.

"If wheat starts flowing through the Black Sea, there's likely more downside for prices," said Rod Baker, an analyst at Bendigo Bank. "If it doesn't, we're getting close to a price floor now."

data.title: Raw sugar gains 1%, white sugar delivery is as expected
data.description:
Raw sugar futures on ICE rose on Friday to post a small weekly gain, with the market finally stabilising after its recent steady fall. Deliveries on the expiration of the spot white sugar contract were as expected at nearly 250,000 metric tons.

The CFTC report on traders' positioning was postponed to Monday due to the Veterans Day holiday.

SUGAR

* Raw sugar ​​settled up 0.19 cent, or 1%, at 18.41 cents per lb. The market had a small weekly gain of 1% after three consecutive weekly declines.

* Dealers said the market was underpinned by a drop in production in Brazil's key centre-south region this season, although weak demand continued to keep a lid on prices.

* They also noted a pickup in buying by China in the physical market.

* White sugar gained 0.9% to $514.40 a metric ton in the last trading day of the December contract (LSUZ6).

* Traders said deliveries against the contract's expiration totalled 244,900 tons, broadly in line with market expectations.

* ED&F Man Commodities was said to be the lone receiver of the sugar while Aditya Commodity Traders and Brazil's BTG were seen among the largest deliverers.

COFFEE

* Arabica coffee settled down 1.05 cent, or 0.4%, at $2.735 per lb. However, it gained 0.7% in the week after a run of three consecutive weekly declines.

* Dealers said supplies of arabica appeared to be improving, boosted partly by strong exports from Brazil, while exchange stocks have also begun to edge higher.

* Exchange stocks stood at 228,586 bags, as of November 12, up from 224,771 bags a week ago. At the same time last year, stocks stood at 404,930 bags.

* Robusta coffee fell 0.3% to $3,196 a ton, hovering just above last week's 2-1/2-year low of $3,140. The market lost 2% weekly.

COCOA

* London cocoa settled up £51, or 1.3%, to £4,037 per ton.

* New York cocoa rose 1.1% to $5,260 a ton.

* Both cocoa markets ended the week flat.

* Weak demand for chocolate has been weighing on prices, although there continue to be concerns that the El Nino weather pattern will curb global production.

data.title: Microsoft Outlook Has Us All in a Chokehold, Apparently — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Emily Russell

Stepping into an elevator at Barron's Midtown Manhattan office yesterday evening, my phone buzzed in my pocket. An ominous text from Mom: "Call me."

My stomach dropped. My parents are in their 60s; an unexpected call could be something serious. I rang her immediately.

"Do you use Outlook?" she said, almost breathlessly.

My mom's Louisiana-based company, she then told me, had suffered a near-total work stoppage since early Thursday afternoon as Microsoft experienced an outage in more than 70 countries. She just wanted to see I had been affected by the tech drama, too.

"No, Mom, I don't use Microsoft Outlook," I said, my anxiety receding.

Luckily, Barron's made the transition from the Microsoft Office suite to Google Workspace years ago. I reassured her that I had dutifully received many, many emails throughout the day — and was even able to reply to a few in between nonstop stories about Nvidia. I swear I heard a billowy sigh of relief on the other end of the phone.

While I escaped Thursday's tech debacle, my mom was far from alone. Hundreds of millions of others that use Microsoft 365 services to email, conduct video calls, and communicate with co-workers were similarly locked out of the software suite at the center of their daily toil, unable to conduct business as usual.

White-collar workers were most obviously affected. Some firms had to cancel their third-quarter earnings calls. Dentists apologized on Facebook, warning patients that their services could be disrupted. The Cleveland Plain Dealer, one of Ohio's biggest newspapers, told readers in a text that it lost its chief way of communicating with the public. When Outlook goes down, the paper wrote, "life gets challenging."

Others had more fun with it. A friend who works at an investment management firm in London said she was "picking her split ends" all day waiting for Microsoft Outlook and Teams to be restored. She also enjoyed some unscheduled TV time: "I've watched, like, five episodes of Vampire Diaries," she said.

The outage was starting to be resolved by midday Friday, more than 24 hours after it started. Microsoft still hasn't said what caused the outage, but said it ruled out malicious activity. (That actually isn't super comforting: If Microsoft is going to go down, I'd rather it be from something largely out of its control, rather than any internal incompetence or infrastructure failures.)

But the aftermath of the outage is far from over. I imagine many workers are spending their Friday afternoons playing email catch-up as Outlook is restored, instead of winding down for the weekend. More importantly, the cost of lost productivity from the outage amounts to at least $7 billion, according to the Anderson Economic Group.

For many Wall Street analysts, tech heads, and news junkies like me, though, Microsoft wasn't the big news of the day. For good reason: Former Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang's affair with an alleged Chinese spy, and the chipmaker's stock subsequent dive, is one of the most consequential and exciting tech stories in recent memory. The scandal compounded the negative AI sentiment that has pummeled tech stocks and unnerved investors in recent weeks.

But the Outlook outage served as a stark reminder that there are technologies the world can actually live without, and those we cannot. We can debate which category AI belongs to, but, after this week, it is clear that Microsoft fits into the latter. That might be why its stock only fell slightly Thursday and has already recovered fully — the market knows we need access to Outlook and PowerPoint, however begrudgingly.

There are alternatives to Microsoft Office, of course, and maybe after this week some businesses will be compelled to explore them. Anthropic recently unveiled Claude Suite, which includes AI-powered tools called Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Meeting. Alphabet offers Google Workspace, with its 3 billion users.

I'm one of those happy 3 billion. But even I couldn't escape the long tentacles of Microsoft this week. I had to cancel a flight Thursday night, in part due to bad weather, but also because I couldn't stomach the prospect of standing in the abnormally long airport security lines that some on social media were reporting and attributing to the outage.

I caught another flight midday Friday. In the security line, the man next to me confirmed Outlook was back up and running. His phone wouldn't stop dinging.

I was reminded that in this new world of otherworldly, intangible technologies like AI and futuristic firms like Nvidia, there is still a special category of things that businesses truly need to do business — like a functioning email inbox. I also remembered how much technology still connects us, too — whether it's a virtual office meeting or communal gripes about said office meeting.

It even gave me a chance to catch up with my family unexpectedly. (But next time your email goes down, Mom, please just text.)

Write to emily.russell@barrons.com.

data.title: Ten-Year Treasury Yield Bounces Back To Highest Level In Almost A Month
data.description:
WASHINGTON (dpa-AFX) - After moving sharply lower over the two previous sessions, treasuries have shown a notable move to the downside during trading on Friday.

Bond prices came under pressure early in the session and have remained firmly negative throughout the day. Subsequently, the yield on the benchmark ten-year note, which moves opposite of its price, has jumped 5.3 basis points to 5.156 percent.

With the strong upward move seen over the past few sessions, the ten-year yield has reached its highest level in almost a month.

The continued weakness among treasuries comes following the release of the Labor Department's report on producer price inflation in the month of October.

While the report showed a slightly smaller-than-expected monthly increase in producer prices, the annual rate of producer price accelerated to 6.5 percent, the fastest pace of growth since November 2022.

'For equities, 6.5% producer inflation matters because companies can get squeezed from both sides,' said Chris Osmond, Chief Investment Officer for Fifth Third Wealth Advisors.

'Persistent input costs pressure margins, while higher bond yields raise the discount rate investors apply to those earnings,' he added. 'That combination puts a much higher hurdle on expensive stocks whose valuations depend on earnings far into the future.'

The report also indicates inflation is broadening beyond energy, as energy prices edged lower but food prices jumped and prices for services increased for a fifth consecutive month.

Following this week's inflation data, the Federal Reserve is widely expected to raise interest rates by at least a quarter point next month, with another quarter point rate in January seen as increasingly likely.

data.title: The Price Tag on Jensen Huang's Resignation: $639 Billion and Counting — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Angela Palumbo

Investors have put a price tag on Jensen Huang's resignation.

Nvidia's stock started falling this week after the New York Times reported on Sunday that Nvidia's board was investigating the CEO after he acknowledged he had been intimate with a business executive believed by U.S. intelligence to be a Chinese spy.

Shares continued their descent after the Times reported on Wednesday there was a second affair, allegedly with an Nvidia executive. Huang resigned from the company Thursday morning.

"Investor confidence is shaken," writes Frank Lee, global head of tech hardware and semiconductor research at HSBC. He downgraded shares of Nvidia to Hold from Buy on Friday.

Investors are working through what they think Nvidia stock is worth without Huang as CEO. The market cap tumbled $639.1 billion this week, its worst weekly decline ever.

Here are some figures to help understand the sheer scope of that drop: that's close to the entire market value of companies like ExxonMobil Holdings and Johnson & Johnson. That's also in line with the total GDP of Norway, Singapore, and the United Arab Emirates.

This underscores how massive Nvidia is and continues to be. And outside of market values, just take a look at what analysts expect fiscal 2028 revenue will be: $694.8 billion.

The stock now sits at the world's third largest company with a $3.86 trillion market cap, behind Microsoft at number two and Apple at number one.

The stock itself is down 13% this week, its worst week since April 4, 2025, according to Dow Jones Market Data. Shares are now sitting at $162.25 and were on pace for their lowest close since July 8, 2025.

The debate now is whether or not investors want to take advantage of the fall. Those who argue against buying the dip believe there is too much unknown about what the company will look like and how it will function in the years ahead without Huang.

Huang has become one of the most prominent figures in the tech space after leading Nvidia to become the number one chip maker for the AI era. He developed important relationships with customers while also being on the front lines of the company's internal tech developments.

"The uncertainties will prevail until a permanent succession plan is laid out and the new CEO is able to demonstrate execution capabilities, writes Lee.

The stock is now trading at 11 times earnings expected over the next 12 months, way below its five year average of 33.6 times. Barron's reported in its latest cover story that Nvidia's earnings have grown at an average annual rate north of 80% for the past five years. For the next three years, Wall Street analysts expect them to grow 40% annually.

This might just be the time to buy.

"Though it's been a shocking few weeks for Nvidia, the worst is most likely behind us, and Tuesday's earnings call should go a long way in providing enhanced investor confidence and share price appreciation," James Demmert, chief investment officer at Main Street Research, wrote on Friday.

Write to Angela Palumbo at angela.palumbo@dowjones.com

data.title: Nvidia Board Reportedly Approached Arm CEO Rene Haas To Succeed Jensen Huang As Top Execs Threaten To Quit, Join SpaceX Terafab
data.description:
Key points:
  • An internal social media letter purportedly signed by Nvidia staff demanded the board's resignation and Huang's reinstatement.
  • Nvidia’s top leadership threatened to quit and join SpaceX Terafab.
  • As the leadership search continues, Nvidia Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress remains at the helm as interim CEO. 

Rene Haas, CEO of Arm Holdings has been reportedly approached by Nvidia’s board to replace Jensen Huang, while an unverified internal memo suggested NVDA employees have threatened to join SpaceX Terafab if Huang is not reinstated.

Haas has led the SoftBank-backed semiconductor designer since 2022. Before leading Arm, he spent roughly seven years working at Nvidia more than a decade ago. Haas maintains robust professional relationships with Huang and several members of Nvidia's board.

While Haas is only one of multiple candidates being evaluated and that no formal offer or acceptance has been finalized, his familiarity with Nvidia’s ecosystem makes him a natural fit, FT reported.

In the interim, Nvidia CFO Colette Kress is managing day-to-day operations as interim CEO. Nvidia did not respond to Stocktwits’ request for comment.

Employee Backlash and SpaceX Terafab Threat

The executive search unfolds amid mounting internal friction. An internal letter circulating on X and allegedly authored by Nvidia employees has severely criticized the board's handling of Huang’s exit.

The missive accuses leadership of negotiating in bad faith and jeopardizing decades of advancement made under Huang’s leadership. The letter also warns that staff may resign to join Elon Musk’s ambitious SpaceX Terafab initiative, noting that Musk has reportedly assured them that open positions await.

“Would be a powerful (and shocking) redemption story if he (Jensen Huang) could be reinstated as CEO ,” Tom Lee, managing partner at Fundstrat Global wrote in a post on X.

Furthermore, an internal “suggestion box” post submitted before Huang’s resignation by a longtime Nvidia engineer urged the company’s board to consider employee sentiment before taking any action, Wired reported.

US Officials Demand Huang’s Testimony

Meanwhile, three House committees have directed Huang to appear for closed-door testimony on December 1, or risk subpoenas, according to an X post by the Select Committee on China. Earlier in the day, CNBC reported Huang had agreed to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving.

Lawmakers are increasing scrutiny after Jensen Huang’s links with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang raised security and defense concerns.

NVDA Stock: Retail View

Retail sentiment on Stocktwits was ‘extremely bullish’ towards Nvidia stock, with ‘extremely high’ retail chatter around the stock.

A user also supported Huang being reinstated as CEO.

View this Stocktwits post

NVDA stock has lost about 13.4% year-to-date.

data.title: Investors Accuse Jefferies, Pershing of Facilitating Massive Fraud in South America — Barrons.com
data.description:
By Kenneth Corbin

A group of 20 investors who say they fell victim to a massive investment fraud are accusing Jefferies and Pershing of failing to take adequate measures to protect them from an unscrupulous South American broker. The investors have filed an arbitration claim against the brokerages, alleging that the central figure in the matter, Sara Goldring, cost them about $16 million in losses. Through a lawyer, she declined to comment.

Goldring, a resident and citizen of Uruguay, controlled two brokerage firms in that country called Custodia de Valores Mobiliarios Corredor de Bolsa, or CVM, and United Brokers, according to a statement of claim filed in an arbitration forum convened by Finra, the brokerage industry's self-regulatory organization.

The claimants accuse Jefferies and Pershing of giving Goldring and her firm "free and unfettered" access to manage clients' money on their platforms, providing a "safe haven" for fraudulent activity that allegedly included churning, cherry-picking, and mismanagement of clients' funds.

For instance, they claim that a Jefferies representative would ask which account to allocate a trade to after it had already been executed, "confirming that Goldring decided which client would bear a position only once its outcome was under way." The claimants say that the trading activity at CVM involved a risky put-options strategy that incurred substantial losses in 2021 and 2022.

A spokeswoman for BNY, Pershing's parent company, acknowledged the arbitration claim but says that the firm hasn't had a chance to review it. "We are aware that claims have been filed but have not received the filing," the spokeswoman says. "We take any allegation of fraud extremely seriously and are committed to conducting a full investigation when we receive the filing."

A spokesman for Jefferies didn't provide a comment on the matter.

Goldring recently pleaded guilty to misappropriation in Uruguay, receiving a two-year sentence of probation, according to media reports and the statement of claim in the Finra proceeding. In the plea agreement, prosecutors said that Goldring used clients' funds for unintended purposes, but didn't pocket money for herself.

$100 million total. Lawyers for the claimants in the case against Jefferies and Pershing allege that Goldring "fraudulently mismanaged" the accounts of more than 700 clients, many of whom were retirees, in Uruguay, Argentina, and Brazil. They peg total losses for all of Goldring's clients at around $100 million.

"This is the next chapter for Goldring's victims," says David Centner, a partner at the law firm Peiffer Wolf, which is representing the claimants. "They have experienced catastrophic losses that have turned their lives upside down, and we aim to prove it wouldn't have been possible without the involvement of the U.S. brokerage and clearing firms Jefferies and Pershing.

Jefferies served as the U.S. introducing broker for Goldring's clients' accounts, with Pershing serving as Jefferies' clearing firm, according to the statement of claim.

That document alleges that the two U.S. brokerage firms ignored numerous red flags that should have alerted them to fraudulent activity and led them to protect investors' funds, including suspicious deposits, trading activity, and the movement of money across accounts.

It describes the claimants as conservative investors with a low-to-moderate tolerance for risk and principal losses. Goldring's brokerage firm allegedly altered these aspects of their investor profiles, including by forging signatures, to accommodate more risk, exploiting weaknesses in Jefferies' and Pershing's systems.

"CVM fabricated hundreds of documents and signatures and grossly misrepresented key details about its customers," the investors allege. "CVM personnel routinely altered signed client documents after the fact to change clients' recorded risk profiles from conservative to aggressive," according to the statement of claim, which says that around 80% of CVM's clients were listed as having an "aggressive" profile.

Goldring's activity has given rise to multiple legal proceedings, including a 2022 appeal by the Central Bank of Uruguay asking Jefferies to pause disbursements from accounts belonging to her and her family members. Jefferies froze the accounts.

Her plea agreement in Uruguay included the forfeiture of $6.8 million held in the United States. In the arbitration case, the claimants are seeking unspecified compensatory and punitive damages, interest, legal fees, and other relief.

Write to advisor.editors@barrons.com

data.title: Son of ex-CIA chief Brennan charged over sexual images of minor girls
data.description:
Key points:
  • Complaint alleges FBI phone review found 88 suspected child pornography images
  • Complaint says investigation began in 2024 after tip to child protection group
  • Virginia authorities searched Kyle Brennan's home in July 2024, complaint says

By Jana Winter and Andrew Goudsward

The son of former CIA Director John Brennan was charged on Friday with "transportation of child pornography," according to court documents and a US law enforcement official.

Kyle Brennan, of Warrenton, Virginia, was charged after an FBI review of his cellphone found 88 images that appeared to depict minor girls engaged in sexually explicit conduct, according to a criminal complaint filed in US District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia.

John Brennan is a longtime antagonist of President Donald Trump, and the Justice Department has been investigating the former CIA director for more than a year.

A criminal complaint showed the investigation into Kyle Brennan began independently of the probe into his father, which has been dubbed by both proponents and detractors the “grand conspiracy” probe.

The complaint said the investigation into the younger Brennan originated in 2024 with a tip to the National Center for Missing & Exploited Children, a child protection organization.

Virginia authorities searched his home in July 2024, and the case was referred to the FBI last month, according to the criminal complaint.

Kyle Brennan was under arrest, and it was not immediately clear if he was represented by an attorney.

John Brennan, who led the CIA during Democratic President Barack Obama’s administration, has been scrutinized as part of a wider probe examining whether law enforcement and intelligence officials violated Trump’s civil rights in prior investigations of the president.

The conspiracy investigation has stalled in recent weeks following the resignations of senior prosecutors who had been overseeing it. No charges have so far been brought.

John Brennan has denied wrongdoing and his lawyers have accused prosecutors of improperly targeting Brennan at Trump’s direction.

The former CIA director was subpoenaed to testify before a grand jury last month, but his appearance was postponed after Joseph diGenova, a DOJ official who had been leading the investigation, resigned in September.

data.title: Wheat Futures Recover on Russia-Ukraine Strife — Daily Grain Highlights
data.description:
By Anthony Harrup

  • Wheat for December delivery rose 1.5% on the Chicago Board of Trade Friday to $5.93 1/4 a bushel as Russia and Ukraine continue strikes after this week's talks failed to produce an agreement to ease Black Sea tensions.
  • Soybeans for January delivery rose 1% to $12.31 1/2 a bushel.
  • Corn for December delivery rose 0.7% to $4.45 1/2 a bushel.

HIGHLIGHTS

Bouncing Back: Wheat futures rebound back from the previous day's losses as Russia and Ukraine step up strikes, with no deal seen to ease Black Sea shipping. Brazil cut its 2026 wheat production estimate to 5.3 million metric tons from 5.7 million tons, while Argentina's Rosario exchange raised its wheat forecast for the country to 24.3 million tons from 23.8 million tons.

Mixed Export Sales: The USDA reported corn export sales of 3.48 million metric tons for last week, including a marketing-year high 2.88 million tons for 2026/27 and 594,400 tons for 2027/28. Soybean sales fell 21% from the week before to 1.15 million tons for 2026/27, with an additional 11,200 tons sold for 2027/28. Wheat export sales fell 66% from the previous week to 182,800 tons, a marketing-year low.

Flash Sales: Private exporters reported sales of 303,300 metric tons of corn to Mexico--272,820 tons for the 2026/27 marketing year and 30,480 tons for 2027/28, the USDA said. In addition, soybean sales for 2026/27 included 134,000 tons to China, 120,000 tons to Vietnam and 100,000 tons to unknown destinations

INSIGHT

More Please: Last week's U.S. corn export sales, equivalent to 113.4 million bushels for 2026/27, were the largest for any week since January and the most on record for the comparable week, said Mike Castle of StoneX. "These are the kind of weeks corn bulls need to see help the weak 2026/27 cumulative sales pace play catch-up." Export sales are still lagging last year by 27.8%, Castle added in a note.

Steady Outlook: Brazilian national supply company Conab held its estimate for the 2026/27 soybean harvest at 181.6 million metric tons, with planting 66.8% complete as of the first week of November. Initial development has been generally positive, but conditions have varied across regions, the state company said. "Irregular rainfall, combined with high temperatures and the effects of the El Niño phenomenon at the start of this cycle, calls for a cautious outlook regarding productive potential." Conab sees corn production from its three harvests reaching 148 million tons, also unchanged from October, with higher planted area compared with last year partially offset by lower yields.

  • Tyson Foods Inc. will release its 4Q 2026 earnings report before the market opens Monday.
  • The USDA will release its weekly Grain Export Inspections report at 11 a.m. ET Monday.
